items.title: We worked at the White House, and we’ve seen these cyber crises before
items.summary:
When flights grounded, banking operations froze, and email went dark, the first question was “Who did it?” Senior officials told Congress they had found no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack. Microsoft traced its failure to a software defect that had gone unnoticed for months; JPMorgan Chase , to a bug in one of its own systems. In each case, systems behaved in ways their operators had not anticipated.

Before we started Atalanta, a mathematical AI company focused on verifying critical systems, we worked at the White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director, where we saw this pattern again and again: the organizations responsible for critical systems could not say with confidence how those systems would behave under normal, abnormal, or hostile conditions.

The hostile case came first. In the opening hours of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, a cyberattack knocked out tens of thousands of modems operated by an American satellite company. Thousands of German wind turbines lost remote monitoring, and users across Europe lost connectivity. The attack made clear that commercial space had become a front line of kinetic conflict, and that Washington needed a clearer picture of the extent to which the industry was exposed.

In 2023, we went directly to industry, meeting roughly 300 operators from 125 space companies across the country. Legacy satellites were operating decades past their design life, and prime contractors had little visibility into the risks introduced by subcontractors. What stuck with us was simple: an attack on one is an attack on all of us.

items.t: We worked at the White House, and we’ve seen these cyber crises before

items.title: Jeff Bezos predicted Amazon would go bankrupt one day. Only one Fortune 500 No. 1 ever has
items.summary:
Amazon is exactly the behemoth you think it is. It streams shows and makes movies, runs grocery stores, rents out cloud computing, builds warehouse robots, and sells home security cameras. Along the way, it has swallowed MGM , Zappos, and Twitch, all on top of the bread-and-butter business of shipping you basically everything.

This June, it took the No. 1 spot on the 2026 Fortune 500 for the first time, ending Walmart ‘s 13-year run at the top. A month later, it topped the 2026 Fortune Global 500 as the world’s largest company by revenue.

That’s not how Jeff Bezos said the story would go. Thirty-two years ago this month, he registered the domain amazon.com for the online bookstore he had incorporated that July as Cadabra Inc. Twenty-four years later, he told employees the company would one day die.

“Amazon is not too big to fail. In fact, I predict one day Amazon will fail. Amazon will go bankrupt. If you look at large companies, their lifespans tend to be 30-plus years, not a hundred-plus years,” Bezos, then CEO, said at a November 2018 all-hands meeting, according to a recording heard by CNBC .

Amazon has now outlived that window and joined a small club. In the Fortune 500 ‘s 72 editions, only four companies have held the No. 1 spot: General Motors, Exxon Mobil, Walmart, and now Amazon. One of them has already done what Bezos predicted.

The one Fortune 500 No. 1 that went bankrupt 

GM sat at No. 1 on the first Fortune 500 in 1955 and held the top spot for decades. In June 2009, it filed for bankruptcy, the largest by an industrial company in U.S. history.

items.t: Jeff Bezos predicted Amazon would go bankrupt one day. Only one Fortune 500 No. 1 ever has

items.title: Can surging corporate profits save the stock market? They just hit 13.4% of GDP—a spike Milton Friedman warned can never last
items.summary:
The stock market took a beating then magically roared back on news that Jensen Huang was being reinstated—giving hope that the AI trade was not lost. But beyond the day to day ups and downs and drama, there’s another force weighing on the market that investors should be paying attention to. Virtually no one on Wall Street even mentions the big structural headwind that, more than any other force, is likely going forward to hold stock returns way, way below the blowout levels we’ve witnessed in recent years. That’s the never-before-seen explosion in earnings that has lifted America’s bottom line so high that it’s probably maxed out, and risks dropping from here. As Sahil Kapoor, executive director of DSP mutual fund in Mumbai, wrote recently, “Historically, these levels of profitability don’t last long. Corporate profitability is the most mean-reverting series in finance.”

The long-term chart of earnings to national income shows just how far the current scenario diverges from past trends. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), the ratio hovered mainly between 6% and 7% from 1945 to 2003. It shot to 10% in the dot.com run-up, cratered in the GFC in 2008 and 2009, and from 2010 to Q2 of last year averaged around 11%.

Starting in mid-2025, the ratio exploded, driven by the likes of Mag 7 profitability, the AI capex explosion that richly benefited software, memory providers, and the Iran war’s windfall to energy producers. In the third quarter, according to government figures released Nov. 25, the ratio hit 13.37%, up from 13.14% in Q2.

items.t: Can surging corporate profits save the stock market? They just hit 13.4% of GDP—a spike Milton Friedman warned can never last

items.title: Trump says he talked Nvidia’s board into reinstating Jensen Huang. It’s not the first company he’s stepped into
items.summary:
In a tumultuous three weeks, Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO following revelations of his affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and at least one Nvidia employee. At the time, the company’s board chair said it did not intend to reinstate him, and Huang remained without an employer for 11 days. Then, the White House intervened. 

President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other senior officials spent this past weekend lobbying on Huang’s behalf, per the Wall Street Journal, and by Monday, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate him as CEO. 

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC in a phone call . “And I convinced them.”

Trump told the Journal that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. Trump said he assured the board his administration wouldn’t punish the company for possible violations of export controls or securities laws if it rehired Huang. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is currently probing the company, just as the Times reported that Trump was briefed in 2025 on Huang’s relationship with the woman on intelligence that she was passing information to Beijing, and chose not to act.

But for the president, his intervention to rescue Huang follows a pattern in which the Trump administration has stepped into corporate America’s affairs. The White House has already bought stakes in companies, obtained veto rights over business decisions, and negotiated terms for chip sales to China—the latter of which has been designated a matter of national security .  For some,  Trump’s intervention in Nvidia, however,…
items.t: Trump says he talked Nvidia’s board into reinstating Jensen Huang. It’s not the first company he’s stepped into

items.title: India uses $1.62 billion in Nepal aid to lock in regional influence—and perhaps ward off China, analysts say
items.summary:
India announced a $1.62 billion economic package for flood-hit Nepal on Nov. 23, pairing reconstruction grants with a credit line for energy projects, the latest move in a decades-old contest with China over the Himalayan country’s future.

The floods that hit Nepal in late August were among the worst disasters in the country’s recorded history, killing at least 1,300 people. An estimated 84,270 people, including over 32,000 children, were affected by the floods, according to UNICEF. 

“It has been three months and families are still working hard to rebuild, but efforts are hampered by the loss of assets and livelihoods they depend on,” Andrea Berardo, the World Food Programme’s deputy country director in Nepal, said in a Nov. 24 statement . “With winter approaching in Nepal’s highlands, many families are still living in temporary shelters and are facing increasingly harsh conditions.”

The money is about more than rebuilding damaged roads and homes. India—already Nepal’s largest trading partner—is using disaster aid to reinforce its ties with a neighbor that China has courted for years, and to keep Nepal’s economic future closely linked to its own, analysts say. 

What’s in the package? 

India’s package to Nepal includes a $377 million grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, along with a $1.24 billion line of credit for energy projects, according to a joint statement by the two countries.

Nepal is likely to use the grant for reconstruction and the credit line—which carries preferential terms and sourcing requirements from India—for…
items.t: India uses $1.62 billion in Nepal aid to lock in regional influence—and perhaps ward off China, analysts say

items.title: Inflation is squeezing Americans so hard that rising grocery bills are now a top reason Black Friday shoppers are cutting back
items.summary:
Black Friday has arrived, and the National Retail Federation expects about 126 million Americans to shop today, part of an estimated 182.7 million who plan to shop over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

But many of those shoppers are heading out with less to spend, with the cost of groceries being a main reason why. Among Black Friday shoppers who are cutting back this year, 68% point to rising grocery costs, up from 57% in 2025, according to a new survey from market research firm Drive Research. Rising living costs are still the top reason, cited by 76%, up from 70%, while 61% blame inflation, up from 54%.

Black Friday budgets are shrinking as a result. Some 41% of Black Friday shoppers expect to spend less on holiday shopping than they did last year, up from 31% in 2025. The share who typically spend $1,000 or more fell to 18% from 24%, and 34% said they feel pressured to spend more on gifts than they can comfortably afford.

Everyday essentials are also on shopping lists. Household necessities like groceries and cleaning supplies are among the planned purchases for 38% of in-person Black Friday shoppers and 31% of those shopping online. Drive Research surveyed 1,405 U.S. adults from Oct. 6 to Oct. 9, and its Black Friday findings are based on the 1,025 respondents who plan to shop over the weekend.

Grocery prices rose 0.4% in October, the biggest monthly increase since April, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics , with beef up 0.9%. Over the 12 months through September, food-at-home prices climbed 1.8%, while overall consumer prices rose 3.7%. Gas has driven…

items.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
items.summary:
Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires

For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.

Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to…

items.title: Crate & Barrel CEO plans a 50-store expansion to win customers from rivals: ‘It’s absolutely a market steal play.’
items.summary:
Few retail CEOs have had a more turbulent run than Janet Hayes. Since taking over Crate & Barrel in 2020, she has steered the furniture retailer through a pandemic and repeated tariff shocks. Now she’s betting the company can come out of it on the offensive.

Hayes hews to the old adage, “Don’t let a good crisis go to waste.” She says she took the tariffs as an opportunity to really understand Crate & Barrel’s supply chain weaknesses and to fix them. On her watch, Crate & Barrel has diversified its supplier base, notably sending more sourcing to Vietnam, and invested in infrastructure and technology to position inventory where it is most likely to sell and better forecast demand. She also moved more upholstery sourcing to the U.S. Crate & Barrel has overhauled everything from its warehouse management software to its e-commerce site. And it now accepts buy-now, pay-later services in an appeal to inflation-pinched consumers.

“You don’t feel it until you’re being tested, but the global supply chain is fragile,” Hayes told Fortune in an interview at the new location of CB2, Crate & Barrel’s sister brand, in New York’s Chelsea district. “You can have the best-laid plans, you can map your ocean liners, you can decide what vendors you’re going to work with, but culture is everything to get through it.”

In her time as CEO, she has worked to flatten decision making at the retailer, to make it more flexible in a furniture market that is, in fact, not growing. “You can get into a command room, but you have to have the people to make it happen,” Hayes says.

items.t: Crate & Barrel CEO plans a 50-store expansion to win customers from rivals: ‘It’s absolutely a market steal play.’

items.title: AI boom or bust? 10 under-the-radar stock picks and investing ideas for either scenario
items.summary:
Investors don’t have to decide whether AI will change the world. They do, however, have to determine how much of their portfolio should depend on it. After all, AI bets now extend far beyond the obvious megacap tech stocks. Utilities and power-equipment makers have been s wept up in the data center build-out . Even parts of the energy sector now trade on the promise that AI will consume an enormous amount of electricity .

The same goes if the bubble bursts—a risk that Nvidia’s recent troubles heighten. Because classic AI stocks are weighted so heavily in indexes like the S&P 500, even a standard 60/40 portfolio can mean betting big on this nascent technology. Investors looking to hedge must find something that doesn’t depend on the very boom they’re worried about.

To help navigate both sides of the trade, Fortune has identified six investment strategies for 2027. Three are built to ride the boom—and three will help you survive a bust.

Boom 

The bet: Picks and shovels 

Ticker: RACK 

The VanEck Data Center Supply Chain ETF allocates to companies that help power, operate, and equip data centers. It’s a bet on the physical infrastructure of the AI boom rather than solely the hyperscalers and software developers themselves.

That’s because the fund gives investors exposure to several layers of the data center supply chain. Think chipmakers, along with companies that make important computing components, like Nvidia , Broadcom , AMD , and Micron . Industrial companies like Eaton , Vertiv , and Johnson Controls that provide the electrical equipment and cooling solutions for…

items.title: 5 trends that will define 2027—and how to invest in them
items.summary:
Heraclitus, the Greek philosopher, is often credited with the idea that the only constant in life is change. He was writing around 500 BC, but he could just as easily have been describing 2027, a year poised to bring seismic shifts in politics, technology, markets, and the way we live and work. Some of what’s coming is already in plain sight, like the AI revolution. Other forces are quieter but could prove just as consequential, including a likely surge in solar construction. Here are the five trends Fortune believes will define the coming year, and how investors can position themselves for each.

Interest rates go even higher 

In 2024, it appeared that pandemic-era inflation had been tamed, and the Federal Reserve responded with a series of cuts to its benchmark interest rate. This optimism didn’t last, however, and price shocks from tariffs and the Iran war led the Fed to boost rates in 2026. The central bank is expected to continue on this path .

This is glum news for homebuyers and the real estate industry, and for sectors including AI, which count on cheap credit to keep their businesses humming. But high interest rates are not bad for everyone. Beneficiaries include individual savers, who can look forward to higher income, and big banks whose business involves lending money.

While banks tend to earn more from loans when rates are higher, it is the “goliath” banks that do best in these environments, said Mike Mayo, head of U.S. large-cap bank research at Wells Fargo Securities. For 2027, Mayo said JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC) , in particular,…
items.t: 5 trends that will define 2027—and how to invest in them

items.title: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it
items.summary:
Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored.

I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every company whose CEO looks irreplaceable.

The sequence of events tells a story.

On November 12, Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation , after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates.

Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.”

Then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government . Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision.

The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished.

That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options.

A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.

Accountability depends…
items.t: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1

When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.”

They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”

items.t: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee

items.title: I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why | Catherine Fookes
items.summary:
Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills

  • Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

  • Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs


This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills, just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK.

The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains.

Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary:
We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.summary:
Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. items.title: Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can attack other energy costs more ruthlessly
items.summary:
Louise Haigh talked the right talk at the CBI this week, but greater ambition and tighter timelines are needed

Shocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027.

Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz.

items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.
